chunks: Al-Haytham ibn Abi Masruq from Abdullah ibn al-Musaddiq from Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Samandarri said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'I am at the gate (meaning the gate of the doors), and they call out for the weapons, so I go out with them.' He said to me, 'Do you see, if you go out and capture a man, and you grant him security (aman), and you give him from the treaty (aqd) what the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) gave to the polytheists, would they pay you for it?' I said, 'No, by Allah, I am your ransom, they would not pay me for it.' He said, 'Then do not go out.' He then said to me, 'Indeed, there is the sword (for those who do not accept the treaty).'

key_terms.اَلسَّيْف: The sword, symbolizing military action or conquest for those who do not accept the treaty
key_terms.اَلْأَمَان: Security or safe conduct granted to a non-combatant or captive
key_terms.اَلْعَقْد: Treaty or covenant, specifically referring to the treaty of peace or submission
key_terms.لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ: To the polytheists, referring to the specific group with whom the Prophet established treaties

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on granting aman and treaty terms to captives during jihad according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the specific conditions under which a captor can demand ransom by granting 'aman' (security), noting that the treaty terms given to polytheists were not accepted for ransom by them. This hadith highlights the distinction between general submission and the specific political-religious treaties of the early Islamic period, emphasizing that the 'sword' (military force) remains the ultimate recourse when such specific terms fail to secure compliance or ransom.
